target.title: Audio-visual speech recognition using deep learning
target.version: published version (Appl Intell 42:722-737; published online 20 December 2014)

read.pdf: Figs. 1-9 captions, axis legends and confusion matrix; Tables 1-4 as represented in text.txt; no figure image or PDF file supplied

entries.text: Corpus: Japanese audiovisual ATR-based dataset, six male speakers, 400 words each (216 phonetically balanced + 184 ATR important words).
entries.condition: Single recording set described per speaker; 24000 word recordings reported (arithmetic unresolved, t67); approximately 1 h of speech in total; Japanese only; no female or child speakers; all six speakers male.
entries.quote: A Japanese audiovisual dataset [23, 51] was used for the evaluation of the proposed models.

entries.text: Audio captured at 16 kHz, 16-bit, one channel in a fixed synchronous audio-visual rig.
entries.condition: 16-bit depth, single channel; laboratory setup with PC, camera, light and microphone (Fig. 1); microphone model, room acoustics, speaker distance and ambient noise level not stated.

entries.text: Audio features are 39 dimensions (13 MFCCs + first + second time derivatives) sampled at 100 Hz to match video.
entries.condition: MFCCs from HTK HCopy; 40-dim log mel filterbank (LMFB) also extracted with the Auditory Toolbox for comparison; 100 Hz frame rate chosen for audio-video synchronisation; MFCC window length, filterbank count, liftering and feature normalisation are not stated (t74).

entries.text: Video is a full-frontal 640 x 480 8-bit monochrome facial view recorded at 100 Hz.
entries.condition: 8-bit monochrome, single full-frontal camera; camera model, lens, distance, lighting control, compression and dropped frames are not stated; no profile or non-frontal views.

entries.text: Mouth region is a manual 128 x 128 crop resized to 64 x 64, 32 x 32 and 16 x 16 for the CNN inputs.
entries.condition: Manual cropping; cropper identity, crop alignment/jitter and tracking stability are not stated; no 128 x 128 CNN condition is reported.

entries.text: Word-level split: 360 training words (2.76e5 samples) and 40 test words (2.91e4 samples) from the same six speakers.
entries.condition: 2.76e5 (2.76×10^5) training samples and 2.91e4 (2.91×10^4) test samples; the sample unit (frame/window/utterance) is not defined; how the 40 words were chosen is not stated (t77); no validation split.
entries.quote: sound signals from 360 training words (2.76×105 samples) and the remaining 40 test words (2.91×104 samples) from six speakers are used to train and evaluate the network, respectively.

entries.text: The paper calls the evaluation 'closed-speaker and open-vocabulary': the 40 test words are unseen in training while the six speakers are shared.
entries.condition: 40 held-out words, same six male speakers as training; 'open-vocabulary' is the paper's term for unseen test words within the fixed 400-word set; no speaker-independent or cross-speaker test anywhere; whether the HMMs themselves are per-speaker is not stated (t76).
entries.quote: yielding a closed-speaker and open-vocabulary evaluation.

entries.text: CNN image pool of 3.05e5 frames is shuffled and split 5/6 train, 1/6 phoneme evaluation (frame level, after augmentation).
entries.condition: 3.05e5 (3.05×10^5) frames drawn from the 360 training words and six speakers; frame-level random split, so adjacent frames from the same word may straddle train/evaluation; no shuffle seed; exact evaluation size not stated (t78); the 40 word-recognition test words are excluded from the CNN image pool, but HMM training features are CNN outputs for words whose frames were 5/6 seen during CNN training.
entries.quote: The image dataset (3.05 × 105 samples) were shuffled and 5/6 of the data were used for training

entries.text: Denoising autoencoder is trained on clean targets from clean plus six noisy variants spanning SNR 30 to -20 dB in 10 dB steps.
entries.condition: 11-frame input windows; targets are the clean features of the same window; artificial Gaussian noise; the training grid (10 dB steps) differs from the evaluation grid (5 dB steps), so the intermediate SNRs are unseen unless the network was retrained (t88).
entries.quote: the signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) was from 30 to −20 dB at 10 dB intervals.

entries.text: At test time the audio input carries artificial Gaussian noise at 11 levels from 30 dB to -20 dB in 5 dB steps, plus clean.
entries.condition: 11 degraded variants plus clean = 12 test SNRs; same protocol in Sec. 6.1 and Sec. 6.5; no real noise, babble, reverberation or channel mismatch is evaluated (t75); how SNR is computed is not stated (t68).
entries.quote: we prepared 11 different deteriorated sound data such that the SNR was 30 dB to −20 dB at 5 dB intervals.

entries.text: CNN phoneme labels are forced alignments from a monophone HMM trained on MFCCs with HTK (39 Japanese phonemes + /sp/ = 40 classes).
entries.condition: Weak supervision: labels inherited from an audio monophone HMM via HTK HVite forced alignment, not hand-labelled; one CNN per speaker; alignment accuracy is never measured; /sp/ frames mostly dropped (t12).

entries.text: Short-pause frames are dropped except five frames adjacent to speech; random shift/rotation copies are added to the image pool.
entries.condition: Augmentation by artificial shifting and rotation of the original images; shift/rotation magnitudes, whether augmented copies are also used at evaluation, and per-class balance are not stated.

entries.text: Denoising autoencoder trained with Hessian-free optimisation in 12 chunks of about 85000 samples per batch.
entries.condition: Hessian-free (Martens) optimisation; L2 weight decay 2.0e-5; sparse random initialisation limited to 15 non-zero incoming weights per unit; biases 0; Core i7-3930K, 32 GB RAM, one GTX Titan with 6 GB; custom CUBLAS library; no epoch count or stopping criterion (t73).

entries.text: CNN trained with SGD on cuda-convnet, mini-batch equal to one-sixth of each speaker's data (about 8500 samples).
entries.condition: Momentum 0.9, learning rate 0.001, weight decay 0.004, zero-mean Gaussian weight initialisation with standard deviation 0.01, biases 0; one model per speaker; no seed, repeated runs or early-stopping set (t47, t73).

entries.text: Seven-layer CNN (C1-P2-C3-P4-C5-P6-F7) with 5 x 5 kernels and one model trained per speaker.
entries.condition: 32/32/64 filters of 5 x 5 pixels; input dimensions 256/1024/4096 for the 16/32/64 resolutions; 40-way softmax; architecture cited to Krizhevsky et al. 2012; parameters empirically determined.

entries.text: Word decoding uses monophone GMM-HMMs with 8/16/32 mixtures for audio features and 1/2/4/8/16/32/64 for visual features.
entries.condition: Single-stream monophone HMM implemented in HTK; visual sweep 1/2/4/8/16/32/64; 360 train words / 40 test words; no language model, lexicon, beam, pruning or grammar settings reported (t51); covariance type and HMM topology also unstated (t84).

entries.text: The MSHMM uses 16 mixture components in each stream and takes state transitions from the audio HMM only.
entries.condition: Audio and visual GMM parameters supply the stream-wise output distributions; the common state-transition probabilities come only from the audio HMM; HTK multi-stream GMM implementation.

entries.text: Audio stream weight is swept manually from 0 to 1.0 in 0.1 steps (visual weight = 1 - audio weight); 11 candidate pairs.
entries.condition: Hand-set rather than learned or adapted online; 11 (gamma_a, gamma_v) pairs; HTK multi-stream GMM; the best pair is selected from the evaluation results (t19).
entries.quote: Audio stream weights γa are manually prepared from 0 to 1.0 at 0.1 intervals.

entries.text: The reported MSHMM rate is the best result over all stream-weight pairs, i.e. the weight is chosen on the evaluation set itself.
entries.condition: No held-out validation data for stream-weight selection: the reported number is the maximum over 11 evaluations on the same 40 test words x 6 speakers.
entries.quote: the best recognition rate is selected from the multiple evaluation results corresponding to all stream weight pairs.

entries.text: Denoised MFCCs give about a 65 % word-recognition-rate gain over original MFCCs under 10 dB SNR; the exact SNR point is not stated.
entries.condition: Unimodal isolated word recognition; 400-word Japanese vocabulary (360 train / 40 test words), six male speakers, closed-speaker, paper-defined 'open-vocabulary'; artificial Gaussian noise under 10 dB SNR (the paper does not say whether this means exactly 10 dB or all points below); 39-dim MFCC input, denoising-autoencoder output; monophone GMM-HMM with 8/16/32 mixtures; no LM; no seeds or repeated runs; whether the gain is absolute or relative is not defined.
entries.quote: demonstrate that approximately 65 % word recognition rate gain is attained with denoised MFCCs under 10 dB

entries.text: MSHMM fusion adds about 10 % word recognition rate over the single-stream HMM with denoised MFCCs under 0 dB SNR; the exact SNR point is not spelled out.
entries.condition: Isolated word recognition, 40 test words x six male speakers, closed-speaker, paper-defined 'open-vocabulary'; audio stream = output of a five-hidden-layer denoising autoencoder, visual stream = CNN phoneme posteriors from 32 x 32 mouth images; 16 GMM mixtures per stream; 0 dB SNR condition (the paper says 'under 0 dB'); best of 11 stream-weight pairs selected on the evaluation set; absolute vs relative gain not defined; no seeds or repeats.
entries.quote: attained an additional 10 % word recognition rate gain under 0 dB SNR for the audio signal input

entries.text: Speaker-averaged visual phoneme recognition is 47.91 % at 64 x 64 input (Table 4).
entries.condition: 40 phonemes (39 Japanese + /sp/), six male speakers p1-p6, averaged with per-phoneme sample normalisation; held-out 1/6 of the 3.05e5-frame image pool; one CNN per speaker; 64 x 64 mouth crop; softmax over 40 classes; no seeds; speaker-wise range 43.57-51.44 (t66).

entries.text: Speaker-averaged visual phoneme recognition is 45.87 % at 32 x 32 input (Table 4).
entries.condition: 40 phonemes, six male speakers, per-phoneme sample-normalised average; held-out 1/6 frame split; per-speaker CNN; 32 x 32 mouth crop; no seeds; speaker-wise range 41.05-50.83.

entries.text: Speaker-averaged visual phoneme recognition is 43.15 % at 16 x 16 input (Table 4).
entries.condition: 40 phonemes, six male speakers, per-phoneme sample-normalised average; held-out 1/6 frame split; per-speaker CNN; 16 x 16 mouth crop; no seeds; speaker-wise range 39.03-47.67.

entries.text: Best visual-only word recognition is about 22.5 % (CNN features at 16 x 16 or 64 x 64, 32 GMM mixtures).
entries.condition: Visual-only isolated word recognition; 40 test words x six male speakers, closed-speaker, paper-defined 'open-vocabulary'; 360 train words; CNN phoneme posteriors as features; monophone HMM with 32 GMM mixtures; best of 35 models (5 feature types x 7 mixture counts); no LM, no seeds.
entries.quote: a rate of approximately 22.5 %, the highest word recognition rate, when a mixture of 32 Gaussian components is used.

entries.text: Per-phoneme visual recognition ranges 30-90 % for vowels versus 0-60 % for all other phonemes.
entries.condition: Mean (and standard deviation in Fig. 5) over six speakers, 64 x 64 input, 40 phoneme classes; consonants largely confused with vowels; no chance level (1/40 = 2.5 %) is stated (t49).

entries.text: Novelty claim: CNN use had been confined to audio signal processing, so CNN-based lipreading is presented as unaddressed.
entries.condition: Positioning claim; no citation to any earlier CNN lipreading system is given.
entries.quote: However, applications of CNNs has been limited to audio signal processing; applications to lipreading remains unaddressed.

entries.text: Claim: CNN-derived phoneme-posterior features beat both image baselines (6 x 6 rescaling and 40-dim PCA) across the reported mixture counts.
entries.condition: Baselines are internal only: 36-dim 6 x 6 rescaled images and 40-dim PCA features (t80); compared over 5 feature types x 7 GMM mixture counts on the same 40 test words x 6 speakers.

entries.text: Conclusion claim: the deep denoising autoencoder effectively filters added noise from clean audio inputs.
entries.condition: Restates the unimodal denoising result; tested only with artificially added Gaussian noise on laboratory recordings; no real-noise condition (t75).

entries.text: Claim: combining modalities improves word recognition, most clearly at low SNR, and is never worse than the better unimodal system.
entries.condition: Based on the curves in Fig. 9; the multimodal number also includes the best-of-11 stream weights selected on the evaluation set; the mixture counts used for the unimodal curves in Fig. 9 are not stated (t85).

entries.text: Abstract claim: the multimodal system adds an extra word-recognition gain for every SNR condition below 10 dB.
entries.condition: No value is given for the below-10 dB gain; the only quantified fusion gain is 10 % at 0 dB (t21).

entries.text: Conclusion claim: reliable AVSR is attained by adaptively switching the information source from audio features to visual features as audio degrades.
entries.condition: The switching is realised only by post-hoc selection of the best fixed stream weight per SNR, not by an online rule; the authors concede automatic selection is lacking (t39).

entries.text: Claim: as audio SNR falls the chosen stream weight moves attention from the audio stream to the visual stream, preventing precision loss.
entries.condition: Read off the lower panels of Fig. 9 (audio stream weight vs SNR); weights are re-selected per SNR on the evaluation results (t19).

entries.text: Claimed main advantage of the MSHMM: explicit control over which observation source (audio or visual) dominates, via stream weights.
entries.condition: Decision-level fusion chosen over feature fusion for simplicity and explicitness; weights are manual (t18).

entries.text: Claimed main advantage of the audio front end: noise-robust features from a rather simple mechanism.
entries.condition: The denoising-autoencoder output replaces conventional enhancement; no comparison with other enhancement techniques is run.

entries.text: Claim: the CNN visual extractor is inherently shift- and rotation-resistant.
entries.condition: Asserted rather than measured; augmentation adds shifted/rotated copies but no direct shift/rotation test is reported; the resolution experiment shows little effect (t45).

entries.text: Conceded: a single CNN over all six speakers degrades precision, so a separate CNN is trained for each speaker.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent visual front end; no cross-speaker evaluation of the visual pathway; raised again in Sec. 7.1 as the current need.

entries.text: Conceded: speaker dependence is attributed to too few lip-region image variations; more images from different speakers are believed necessary.
entries.condition: Footnote 1 of Sec. 5.2; the corpus itself holds only six male speakers and about 1 h of speech.

entries.text: Conceded: automatic, adaptive stream-weight selection in response to audio reliability is unsolved and blocks real-world use.
entries.condition: Stream weights are hand-set and swept offline (t18) and chosen on the evaluation set (t19).
entries.quote: automatic and adaptive selection of the stream weight in relation to changes in audio input reliability becomes an important issue to be addressed.

entries.text: Conceded: forced-alignment phoneme targets are inadequate, especially for short consonants, and label acquisition must be improved.
entries.condition: Consonant labels are time-critical and consonant training samples are far fewer than vowel samples; label accuracy itself is never measured.

entries.text: Conceded: consonants are usually misread as vowels because tongue, teeth and oral-cavity gestures are invisible in frontal video.
entries.condition: Sensing limitation of a single frontal monochrome camera; the effect is visible in the Fig. 6 confusion matrix.

entries.text: Conceded: bilabial consonants /m/, /p/, /b/ are not recognized as well as visually expected.
entries.condition: These were expected to be the best-discriminated class for lipreading, yet performance is below expectation (Figs. 5 and 6).

entries.text: Conceded: a DNN-HMM would estimate state posteriors better than the GMM-HMM used here; the primary stated reason for choosing GMM-HMM was seamless MSHMM integration.
entries.condition: The acknowledged-stronger hybrid alternative is not run as a baseline anywhere in the paper.

entries.text: Conceded: increasing the number of GMM mixture components produces only slight differences, which the authors call not significant.
entries.condition: Stated in identical words in Sec. 6.1 and Sec. 6.5; no statistical test is reported.

entries.text: Conceded: input image resolution has no prominent effect on visual word recognition.
entries.condition: Contradicts any expectation that higher-resolution mouth crops help; 16 x 16 and 64 x 64 tie for the best word rate (t25); Fig. 5 and Fig. 8 captions also miscount the resolutions/features (t82, t64).

entries.text: Conceded: only static laboratory conditions were tested; reverberation, illumination and facial-orientation changes remain unevaluated.
entries.condition: Named as future work in the conclusion; no real-world or in-the-wild evaluation appears in the paper.

entries.text: No seeds, number of runs, confidence intervals or variance are reported for any word-recognition result; the only SD is across six speakers in Fig. 5.
entries.condition: Word-recognition figures are single-run curves; the phoneme standard deviations are across speakers, not across training runs.
entries.quote: Figure 8 shows the word recognition rates acquired from 35 different models

entries.text: Word-recognition rates are never defined: pooling versus per-speaker averaging, and the metric itself (accuracy vs 1 - WER), are left unstated (only phoneme rates are said to be sample-normalised).
entries.condition: It cannot be determined whether the Fig. 3/4/8/9 curves are means over 240 test tokens, per-speaker means, or something else.

entries.text: No chance level or random-guess baseline is given for the 400-word vocabulary or the 40-class phoneme task.
entries.condition: The only reported baselines are the system's own original-MFCC and image-based features; 1/400 word and 1/40 phoneme (2.5 %) chance levels are never stated.

entries.text: No comparison against prior AVSR systems or any public benchmark: only internal baselines are run.
entries.condition: Internal baselines only: original MFCCs, 6 x 6 rescaled images, 40-dim PCA features, unimodal versus MSHMM; no number from cited AVSR work is reproduced.

entries.text: No language model, lexicon constraint, beam/pruning setting or decoder configuration is reported for word decoding.
entries.condition: Decoding is described only as monophone GMM-HMMs with given mixture counts; nothing else about the decoder is specified.

entries.text: No confirmation stage (confidence-based accept/reject, user verification of recognised words) is described anywhere.
entries.condition: The pipeline runs sensor -> feature extractors -> multi-stream HMM -> isolated word, with no confirmation step.

entries.text: No correction, feedback or on-line re-training mechanism at use time is described.
entries.condition: No error correction, no user feedback loop, no incremental adaptation of any component.

entries.text: No validation or selection set is described: network depth, read-out style and image resolution were chosen empirically.
entries.condition: Model selection appears to reuse the same 40 test words (and for stream weights explicitly the evaluation results, t19); no held-out tuning data is named.
entries.quote: Parameters for the network structures are empirically determined with reference to previous studies [18, 21].

entries.text: Word-recognition results are given only as plotted curves; no numeric table of word recognition rates is provided.
entries.condition: Apart from the two prose gains (65 % under 10 dB, 10 % under 0 dB) and the 22.5 % visual-only maximum, rates must be read off Figs. 3, 4, 8 and 9.

entries.text: Output unit is the isolated word from a 400-word vocabulary; the CNN's 40-way phoneme posterior is only an intermediate representation.
entries.condition: No continuous speech, no sentence-level output, no word-level language model; the visual pathway emits phoneme posteriors consumed by the HMM.

entries.text: The CNN emits a 40-way softmax over 39 Japanese phonemes plus short pause /sp/.
entries.condition: Last-layer posterior probabilities are recorded as the visual feature sequence fed to the HMM; /sp/ included as a class.

entries.text: All data come from one controlled laboratory capture; no deployment or field test is reported.
entries.condition: PC, camera, light and microphone in a fixed synchronous rig (Fig. 1); no wearable, robot or moving-speaker condition.

entries.text: Denoised features are the autoencoder's output for an 11-frame input window (429 = 11 x 39 input dimensions).
entries.condition: The middle frame of the 11-frame output is taken as the feature (SequenceOut); BottleNeck and SingleFrameOut read-outs are compared in Sec. 6.1; the five-hidden-layer straight network (Table 1(d)) is used in the AVSR run.
entries.quote: the neuronal outputs of the deep autoencoder when 11 frames of audio features are provided as input.

entries.text: Claim: MFCC inputs generally outperform log mel-filterbank inputs across the SNR sweep (Fig. 3).
entries.condition: Comparison over 12 SNR points, three GMM mixture counts and several read-out types, all on the same 40 test words x 6 speakers.

entries.text: Claim: the five-hidden-layer denoising autoencoder gives the best noise-robust word recognition at every SNR among the four depths tested.
entries.condition: Depths 1, 3, 5 and 7 tested with MFCC input; the winning depth is then fixed for all AVSR experiments (t21); selection is made on the same evaluation curves, with no held-out data.
entries.quote: autoencoder with five hidden layers obtained the best noise robust word recognition performance among all SNR ranges.

entries.text: GMM-HMM rather than DNN-HMM was chosen primarily so that the MSHMM could be applied seamlessly as the integration mechanism.
entries.condition: Design rationale, not an accuracy comparison; no DNN-HMM baseline is reported (cf. t43).

entries.text: Visual features for the word-recognition experiment are said to come from 216 training words, while every experiment section says 360 training words; the discrepancy is never explained.
entries.condition: Sec. 5.2 states 216 training words for CNN feature generation; Sec. 6.4 and Sec. 6.5 state 360 training words for HMM and MSHMM training; 216 is also the count of phonetically balanced words in the corpus.
entries.quote: mouth area image sequences corresponding to 216 training words

entries.text: Fig. 8's caption counts six visual features including four CNN resolutions, while the body reports five feature types and the tables define only three trimmed resolutions; the mismatch is not reconciled.
entries.condition: Caption counts 2 image-based + 4 CNN features over four resolutions; body text and legend show 5 types (6 x 6, PCA, CNN 16/32/64) and 35 models = 5 x 7.

entries.text: PCA of the 40-dim CNN phoneme-posterior sequences retains 31.1 % cumulative variance in 40 components; the first three PCs are plotted.
entries.condition: 64 x 64 mouth images; 40-dim posteriors from a per-speaker CNN; five Japanese vowels /a/, /i/, /u/, /e/, /o/; test image sequences from six speakers; PCA fitted on the extracted posterior sequences; no seed or separate PCA train/test detail.

entries.text: At 64 x 64, speaker-wise phoneme recognition ranges from 43.57 % (p4) to 51.44 % (p6).
entries.condition: Table 4, 64 x 64 input, 40 phonemes, six male speakers p1-p6; speaker-averaged value 47.91 %; single value per speaker, no run-to-run SD.

entries.text: Corpus arithmetic is inconsistent: 400 words x six speakers = 2400 utterances, but the paper reports 24000 recordings; the per-word sample counts imply about 2400 utterances, so either a zero is wrong or a repetition factor is unstated.
entries.condition: Derived from 360 training words x 6 speakers and 2.76e5 samples (~128 samples/word) and 40 test words x 6 speakers and 2.91e4 samples (~121/word); the paper says 'one set of words per speaker' and never states repetitions.
entries.quote: In total, 24000 word recordings were prepared

entries.text: The SNR definition and noise realisation are unstated: no formula (global vs frame-level), noise seed, or per-utterance noise draw is given.
entries.condition: Noise is described only as 'several strengths of Gaussian noises' superimposed on the original signals; training uses 10 dB steps and evaluation 5 dB steps (t88), but how SNR is measured is not stated.

entries.text: Novelty claim: the CNN visual front end needs no dedicated lip-shape models or hand-labelled training data.
entries.condition: Asserted as a main advantage; in practice mouth regions are manually cropped and phoneme targets come from HTK forced alignment, so the pipeline still needs manual crops and an audio HMM.

entries.text: Contribution: an AVSR system that couples a deep denoising autoencoder for audio, a CNN for visual phoneme prediction, and an MSHMM for fusion and isolated-word recognition.
entries.condition: System-level novelty claim; each component is adapted from prior work (denoising autoencoder [48, 49], CNN [27], MSHMM [6, 7, 20]); no end-to-end joint training.
entries.quote: This study introduces a connectionist-hidden Markov model (HMM) system for noise-robust AVSR.

entries.text: Read-out comparison: SingleFrameOut is best at high SNR, SequenceOut overtakes at low SNR, and BottleNeck barely improves on the original features.
entries.condition: Compared over 12 SNRs and 8/16/32 GMM mixtures in Fig. 3; the winning read-out is not fixed for the AVSR run, which instead uses the five-hidden-layer straight SequenceOut network.

entries.text: Conceded: the bottleneck read-out improves only slightly over the original input at middle SNR, and the advantage is scarce.
entries.condition: Same Fig. 3 comparison; BottleNeck is not used in the final AVSR system.

entries.text: No training schedule is given: neither the number of epochs/updates nor a convergence or early-stopping criterion is reported for the autoencoder or the CNN.
entries.condition: Only optimizer hyperparameters are listed (Hessian-free chunks, SGD momentum/learning rate/weight decay); no iteration count, stopping rule or held-out early-stopping set.

entries.text: No feature normalisation is described: no CMVN/mean-variance normalisation of MFCCs or intensity normalisation of mouth images, and MFCC window/filterbank/liftering details are omitted.
entries.condition: Only 13 MFCCs plus first and second derivatives (39 dims) via HTK HCopy are specified; image cropping is manual but no photometric normalisation is stated.

entries.text: Only artificial Gaussian noise is evaluated; no real noise, babble, reverberation, channel or microphone mismatch condition is tested.
entries.condition: All degraded audio is generated by superimposing Gaussian noise on the original clean recordings; real-world robustness is deferred to future work (t46).

entries.text: It is not stated whether the GMM-HMMs are trained per speaker or pooled across the six speakers; only the CNN is explicitly per-speaker.
entries.condition: The paper says training uses 360 words and evaluation 40 words 'from the same speaker', but never specifies whether the audio or visual HMM is speaker-specific.

entries.text: How the 40 test words were chosen from the 400-word list is not stated, nor whether the split was fixed before seeing results.
entries.condition: The split is only described as 360 training and the 'remaining' 40 test words; no randomisation, stratification or seed is given.

entries.text: The exact size of the held-out phoneme evaluation set is not stated; only 5/6 training and the remaining 1/6 of 3.05e5 frames are given.
entries.condition: No exact frame count for the evaluation split, no seed for the shuffle, and no guarantee that frames from the same word do not straddle the split.
entries.quote: The image dataset (3.05 × 105 samples) were shuffled and 5/6 of the data were used for training

entries.text: Autoencoder configurations tested: 429-dim input/output with bottleneck 300-150-80-40-80-150-300 (a), 429-to-39 triangle 300-150-80 (b), and straight 429-429 networks of 7/5/3/1 layers (c-f).
entries.condition: Table 1; the AVSR system uses the five-hidden-layer straight network (d), 300-300-300-300-300; 11-frame windows give 429 = 11 x 39.

entries.text: Visual word-recognition baselines are a 36-dim 6 x 6 rescaled image feature and a 40-dim PCA feature; CNN posteriors are compared against them over seven GMM mixture counts.
entries.condition: 35 models = 5 feature types x 7 mixture counts; no external AVSR baseline; the 6 x 6 and PCA features are computed from the same mouth crops.

entries.text: Implementation uses cuda-convnet for the CNN and HTK for HMM/alignment; no public code or scripts are linked.
entries.condition: Open-source tools named but no repository URL, version commit or training script; cuda-convnet cited to Krizhevsky et al. 2012; custom CUBLAS library for the autoencoder.

entries.text: Fig. 5 caption states four input image resolutions, but only 16 x 16, 32 x 32 and 64 x 64 are defined, tabulated and plotted; the fourth is never identified.
entries.condition: Table 4 has three rows; Sec. 4 defines three resized crops; Fig. 5 legend lists 16x16/32x32/64x64.

entries.text: Under the 2400-utterance reading of the corpus (t67), each SNR condition scores 40 words x six speakers = 240 word tokens, with one token per word/speaker and no repetition.
entries.unit: word tokens per SNR (derived, conditional on t67)
entries.condition: Derived from 40 test words and six speakers and the stated 'one set of words per speaker'; if the 24000 figure is literal, the token count would be 2400. No per-token breakdown, CI or repetition detail is reported.

entries.text: GMM covariance type, HMM topology/state count, parameter tying and HTK training iterations are not reported.
entries.condition: Only mixture counts and monophone units are given; decoder settings are absent too (t51).

entries.text: The mixture counts used for the unimodal curves in Fig. 9 are not stated; the MSHMM uses 16 per stream while the unimodal sweeps use 8/16/32 (audio) and 1-64 (visual).
entries.condition: The paper says the unimodal models are identical to 'Original' and '5 layers' in Figs. 3 and 4, which sweep mixture counts, but does not state which count is used in the Fig. 9 comparison.

entries.text: Sec. 6.5 describes the audio stream as autoencoder outputs 'when clean MFCCs are provided as inputs', leaving unclear whether the denoiser is applied to the noisy test features.
entries.condition: The method in Sec. 5.1 trains on noisy inputs and clean targets, and the noise-robustness claim implies noisy test inputs, but the AVSR section does not restate that the test-time input is noisy.
entries.quote: For sound features, we utilized the neuronal outputs of the straight-shaped deep denoising autoencoder with five hidden layers

entries.text: Sec. 5.1 says six deteriorated variants plus the clean signal (seven total), but the next sentence says the features come from 'eight variations'; no eighth variant is identified.
entries.condition: The SNR grid 30, 20, 10, 0, -10 and -20 dB gives six noisy variants; adding the clean signal gives seven, not eight, and no other variation is described. Sec. 6.5 later evaluates 11 noisy variants plus clean at 5 dB steps (t88), so 'eight' matches neither count.

entries.text: The denoiser is trained on six noise levels at 10 dB steps but evaluated on 11 levels at 5 dB steps; the intermediate SNRs may never have been seen in training and the paper does not say.
entries.condition: Sec. 5.1 prepares six deteriorated variants at 10 dB intervals (30 to -20 dB); Sec. 6.5 evaluates at 5 dB intervals (11 levels). No statement that training covered the intermediate levels or that the autoencoder was retrained.
entries.quote: such that the SNR was 30 dB to −20 dB at 5 dB intervals

entries.text: The authors claim their approach avoids dedicated lip-shape models and hand-labeled training data.
entries.condition: Claim applies to the proposed bottom-up CNN visual feature extractor.

questions.q: How large is the claimed denoising gain, and on exactly what test condition does it rest?
questions.answer: About 65 % word-recognition-rate gain for denoised MFCCs over original MFCCs under 10 dB SNR (the exact SNR point is not stated), measured in isolated-word recognition on a 400-word Japanese vocabulary (360 train / 40 held-out words) from six male speakers in the paper's 'closed-speaker and open-vocabulary' protocol (fixed 400-word set with 40 unseen test words), with artificial Gaussian noise, a monophone GMM-HMM with 8/16/32 mixtures, no language model and no seeds or repeated runs; the paper does not say whether the gain is absolute or relative, and the number appears only as prose plus the curves of Fig. 3.

questions.q: How much does visual fusion add, and how was the fusion weight chosen?
questions.answer: 10 % word-recognition gain under 0 dB SNR versus a single-stream HMM on denoised MFCCs; audio stream weights are hand-swept from 0 to 1.0 in 0.1 steps and the reported figure is the best over all 11 pairs, i.e. selected on the evaluation set itself, with no held-out validation data (t19, t54). The abstract additionally claims an extra gain for all SNRs below 10 dB without giving a value, and the paper leaves the absolute/relative gain base and the mixture counts used for the Fig. 9 unimodal curves unstated.

questions.q: What visual-only numbers does the paper report, and against what baselines?
questions.answer: Phoneme level: 43.15 % (16 x 16), 45.87 % (32 x 32) and 47.91 % (64 x 64) speaker-averaged over 40 phonemes on a held-out frame split with a per-speaker CNN. Word level: about 22.5 % best (CNN features with 32 GMM mixtures). Baselines are internal only (36-dim 6 x 6 rescaling, 40-dim PCA); no prior AVSR system or public benchmark is compared and no chance level is given, while bilabials perform worse than expected.

questions.q: Which evaluation conditions does the paper leave unstated?
questions.answer: Seeds, repetitions and uncertainty (t47); aggregation and definition of word rates (t48); chance level (t49); external baseline (t50); language model and decoder settings (t51); any confirmation stage (t52); any correction stage (t53); validation/selection data (t54); numeric tables of word rates (t55); SNR definition and noise realisation (t68); training epochs/stopping (t73); feature normalisation and MFCC details (t74); real-noise conditions (t75); whether the HMMs are per-speaker (t76); test-word selection (t77); exact phoneme-evaluation size (t78); GMM covariance/topology (t84); mixture counts in the Fig. 9 comparison (t85); whether the denoiser is applied to noisy test features (t86); plus reporting inconsistencies in 216 versus 360 training words (t63), the Fig. 8 feature count (t64), the corpus count (t67), the Fig. 5 resolution count (t82), the sound-signal variation count (t87) and the training/evaluation SNR-grid mismatch (t88).

questions.q: What limitations do the authors themselves concede?
questions.answer: Speaker-dependent CNNs, one per speaker, attributed to too few lip-image variations (t37, t38); no automatic or adaptive stream-weight selection (t39); forced-alignment phoneme labels needing improvement for consonants (t40); consonants misread as vowels because oral-cavity gestures are invisible (t41); bilabials worse than expected (t42); DNN-HMM acknowledged as advantageous over the GMM-HMM used (t43); mixture-count effect not significant (t44); image-resolution effect not prominent (t45); bottleneck read-out advantage scarce (t72); real-world reverberation, illumination and facial-orientation conditions unevaluated (t46).

No. It is closed-speaker and, in the paper's terms, 'open-vocabulary': the same six male speakers appear in training and test and only words are held out (360/40); 'open-vocabulary' here means the 40 test words are unseen, not that the vocabulary is unbounded, since the task is a fixed 400-word set. The visual front end is trained separately per speaker because a single shared CNN degraded precision. Whether the audio and visual HMMs are per-speaker is not stated.

questions.q: Can a reviewer quote exact word-recognition rates for each SNR point?
questions.answer: No: word results are plotted only (Figs. 3, 4, 8, 9) with no numeric table. The exact word-level figures stated in prose are the approximately 65 % denoising gain under 10 dB, the 10 % fusion gain under 0 dB and the approximately 22.5 % visual-only maximum; every other SNR point would have to be read off a figure.

questions.q: What does the paper claim as novel or superior?
questions.answer: That CNN-based lipreading had been left unaddressed (t27); a system coupling a denoising autoencoder, a CNN and an MSHMM (t70); that no lip-shape models or hand-labelled data are needed (t69); that CNN phoneme-posterior features beat image baselines (t28); that MFCCs beat log mel filterbanks (t60); that a simple denoising autoencoder yields noise-robust features (t35, t29); that the five-hidden-layer autoencoder is best across all SNRs (t61); that SingleFrameOut wins at high SNR while SequenceOut wins at low SNR (t71); that the CNN is shift- and rotation-resistant (t36); and that the MSHMM gives explicit stream-weight control over the information source while staying at least as good as the better unimodal system (t34, t32, t33, t30).

questions.q: Are the reported setup details internally consistent?
questions.answer: No. Sec. 5.2 says the visual features for the isolated-word experiment come from 216 training words while Sec. 6.4/6.5 say 360 training words (t63); the Fig. 8 caption counts six visual features over four resolutions while the body reports five feature types over three trimmed resolutions and 35 models (t64); the corpus reports 24000 recordings although 400 words x six speakers gives 2400 utterances, and the per-word sample counts imply the smaller figure (t67); and the Fig. 5 caption says four image resolutions although only three are defined and plotted (t82); Sec. 5.1 also counts eight sound-signal variations where six noisy variants plus the clean signal gives seven (t87).

questions.q: What code or implementation is available, and does it add any undisclosed evaluation conditions?
questions.answer: No public repository or training/evaluation script is linked. The paper names cuda-convnet for the CNN, HTK for HMM/alignment and a custom CUBLAS library for the autoencoder, so no code-only conditions (splits, seeds, normalisation, selection data) could be checked; the read.code field is null.

questions.q: Is the corpus size arithmetically consistent with the stated protocol?
questions.answer: No. 400 words x six speakers gives 2400 utterances, yet the paper reports 24000 recordings and says 'one set of words per speaker'. The per-word sample counts (2.76e5 for 360 training words, 2.91e4 for 40 test words, over six speakers) imply about 128 and 121 samples per word, i.e. roughly 2400 utterances, so either the 24000 figure has an extra zero or an unstated repetition factor exists. Each SNR condition therefore scores about 240 word tokens if the smaller count is right, or 2400 if the 24000 figure is literal.

questions.q: Are the reported percentage gains absolute or relative?
questions.answer: Undefined. The paper states a 65 % 'word recognition rate gain' under 10 dB SNR and a 10 % 'word recognition rate gain' under 0 dB SNR but never says whether these are absolute percentage-point improvements or relative improvements over the baseline; the curves are the only way to check, and no numeric table is given.
